tldr: We developed "DITTO-X," a teleoperation exoskeleton with haptic and force feedback for multi-fingered hands. It works across multiple robot hands and introduces "reverse teleoperation," which back-drives human fingers to match the robot's joint angles during autonomous policy deployment, preventing operators from dropping grasped objects during interventions.
hero_caption: Hardware design of DITTO-X. Building on a prior design that covered only the thumb and index finger, it adds a 3-DoF middle finger module. It also embeds linear resonant actuators (LRAs) at the fingertips to convey transient contact events via vibration, delivering both continuous force feedback and transient contact cues.
overview:
In dexterous manipulation with robot hands, teleoperated human demonstrations are the backbone of imitation learning. Human intervention—where an operator takes over control to recover from an impending failure during autonomous execution—is also essential for interactive learning methods like DAgger to refine policies. However, most existing teleoperation systems rely solely on visual feedback or are designed around two-finger parallel-jaw grippers. With multi-fingered hands, frequent occlusions from the hand and arm, combined with the inability to sense contact force or slip through vision alone, make delicate manipulation and force regulation extremely difficult.

This becomes even more severe during human interventions into autonomous policies. When a human tries to suddenly take over while the robot is already grasping a tool or a soft object, joint angle mismatches between the human hand and the robot hand often cause the object to be dropped or crushed right at the handover moment.

To solve this, the authors propose the multi-fingered exoskeleton interface "DITTO-X." DITTO-X delivers real-time contact sensations to the operator using motor-driven joint torque feedback and fingertip vibrotactile cues. Furthermore, it introduces "reverse teleoperation," using the exoskeleton's actuators to actively back-drive the operator's fingers into the autonomous robot hand's current configuration. Because the human hand is already aligned with the robot's grasping pose before taking over, the operator can seamlessly assume control without dropping objects. Real-robot experiments demonstrated higher demonstration data collection throughput and dramatic performance gains in policy learning using intervention data.
contributions: Built a hand-agnostic teleoperation framework with force and haptic feedback that supports three commercial five-finger hands with different degrees of freedom (Sharpa, Wuji, and Inspire) without per-hand redesign.

Realized a dual-layer tactile feedback loop combining continuous joint torque rendering for sustained grip force and fingertip LRA vibrations for transient contact events, enabling operators to perceive object properties even under visual occlusion.
Proposed "reverse teleoperation," which forces the human hand via the exoskeleton to follow the autonomous robot's configuration, enabling seamless control transfer while preserving the grasp state.
Open-sourced all hardware designs, control software, and training pipelines, along with over 1,800 contact-rich manipulation episodes collected across the three robot hands.

sections.heading: Challenges in dexterous teleoperation and human intervention: What was missing?
sections.summary: Multi-finger teleoperation has suffered from kinematic mismatches and limited haptic feedback, while intervention-based learning (such as DAgger) faces discontinuities during control transfer. This paper tackles both challenges simultaneously using hand-agnostic force-haptic feedback and reverse teleoperation that aligns the human to the robot.
sections.details:
### Dexterous Teleoperation and Haptic Feedback
Teleoperation of dexterous multi-fingered hands has been extensively studied from the viewpoint of geometric kinematic alignment, using vision-based hand tracking, leader-follower mechanisms, and learning-based retargeting. However, most of these methods cannot return force or contact sensations, forcing operators to guess interactions solely from visual changes. While motorized exoskeleton gloves do exist, actuator packaging constraints often limit them to 1-DoF feedback per finger or reduce forces to task-space vectors, failing to intuitively convey how much load is applied to which joint. Its predecessor, DITTO, achieved joint-level force feedback, but it was limited to two fingers and required identical 1:1 leader-follower kinematics, making it incompatible with diverse commercial five-finger hands.

### Shared Autonomy and the Difficulty of Intervention
Shared autonomy frameworks where robots act autonomously and humans take over only near failure (like DAgger) have gained traction for efficient data collection. Yet most prior work focuses on *when* to intervene (intervention timing), overlooking the physical handover problem of *how* to intervene smoothly. While transition transients during control handovers are well known in autonomous driving, the issue is far harsher for multi-fingered hands. At the moment of intervention, the robot is often already holding a tool or a fragile object. Any discrepancy between the controller's target configuration and the human's hand pose instantly drops or crushes the object, catastrophically failing the task.

sections.heading: DITTO-X mechanism design and the mechanics of "reverse teleoperation"
sections.summary: DITTO-X drives the thumb, index, and middle fingers with motors and couples the ring and little fingers to the middle finger, adapting to diverse five-finger hands. Along with dual-layer tactile feedback combining sustained joint torque and fingertip vibration, it implements "reverse teleoperation" to trace the robot's pose onto the human hand.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-A1: Position Retargeting Across Heterogeneous Kinematics
DITTO-X aligns its motors with the anatomical joint axes of the human hand. By introducing a new middle finger module, it independently actuates three fingers, while coupling the robot's ring and pinky fingers to the middle finger's motion. This accommodates a wide spectrum of grasps, from dexterous pinches to power grasps. For the index and middle fingers, the MCP joint's flexion and adduction/abduction and the PIP joint's flexion map 1:1 to the robot hand, allowing direct joint angle transfer. For the thumb, which has substantial structural differences, the system tracks its tip position in a palm-relative Cartesian coordinate frame (task space), applies a scaling factor $s_f$, and solves inverse kinematics (IK).

### III-A2: Force and Haptic Feedback Loops for Heterogeneous Sensing
Feedback is synthesized based on the data available from the robot (motor currents or fingertip tactile sensors). For 1:1 mapped joints, joint torque estimated from current $\hat{\tau}_f$ is directly set as DITTO-X's desired torque $\hat{\tau}^{\mathrm{des}}_l$. For non-1:1 fingers like the thumb, fingertip force is estimated via the robot's Jacobian $J_f$ as $\hat{F}_f = (J_f^\top)^\dagger \hat{\tau}_f$, and mapped to exoskeleton joint torques via DITTO-X's Jacobian $J_l$. These torques pass through a low-pass filter, and a control law with gains $k_j$ and thresholds $\tau_{\mathrm{th},j}$ drives the exoskeleton motors. Furthermore, to capture transient contact events, linear resonant actuators (LRAs) are mounted on the fingertips. A contact detection threshold with hysteresis ($F_{\mathrm{rising}} < F_{\mathrm{falling}}$) triggers a 0.5-second decaying vibration only on rising contact, successfully combining sustained grip force perception (motor torques) with transient contact detection (vibrations).

### III-B: "Reverse Teleoperation" for Smooth Interventions
During autonomous policy execution, DITTO-X inverse-maps the robot hand's commanded joint angles to the human exoskeleton, actively driving the operator's fingers into the robot's current pose. Even when the human presses an intervention key, control is not handed over immediately. Control transfers only when the operator actively moves their fingers beyond a threshold $\delta_{\mathrm{release}}$ away from the robot's target pose. This prevents erratic behaviors from accidental inputs and enables smooth takeovers without any postural discontinuity, even when an object is already grasped.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: From haptic discrimination to DAgger policy improvement
sections.summary: We conducted vision-free object discrimination user studies (T1, T2) and manipulation and intervention tasks using tongs (T3, T4). Furthermore, we evaluated imitation learning and DAgger performance improvements across three contact tasks requiring delicate force regulation.
sections.details:
### User Study Setup
Six healthy participants completed four tasks, comparing DITTO-X against a commercial magnetic tracking glove, Manus Pro (no force/haptic feedback, no reverse teleoperation), as a baseline.
- **T1 (Size Discrimination)**: With eyes closed, participants grasp cylinders of different diameters (30, 50, 70 mm) using the robot and identify the size using tactile cues alone.
- **T2 (Compliance Discrimination)**: Similarly with eyes closed, participants identify whether an object is soft, rigid, or if the grasp missed (free space).
- **T3 (Full Trajectory Tong Manipulation)**: Pick up tongs, grasp a toy with them, and transport it to a target location.
- **T4 (Intervention on a Trained Policy)**: After an autonomous policy picks up the tongs, the human takes over to complete grasping and placing the toy.

### Policy Learning and DAgger Setup
A Sharpa hand was mounted on a Franka Panda arm, with end-effector pose tracked via a Meta Quest 3S. We evaluated three tasks: "Battery Insertion" (pushing against a spring force), "Tong Manipulation" (where improper force drops the object), and "Raspberry Grasping" (easily crushed). Policies were trained using Diffusion Policy (UNet variant), taking end-effector pose, joint angles, camera images, and tactile sensor readings as inputs. After collecting pre-training demonstrations for each task, we ran two rounds of DAgger where humans intervened during autonomous rollouts, evaluating success rate trajectories.

sections.heading: Results: Force-haptic benefits and major gains from reverse teleoperation
sections.summary: Combining force and haptics achieved 86–91% vision-free object discrimination. In tong intervention tests, DITTO-X achieved a 78.3% success rate, crushing Manus (27.7%). Furthermore, policies fine-tuned with reverse-teleoperated intervention data showed substantial performance gains.
sections.details:
### User Study Results
In object discrimination, enabling both force feedback and vibrotactile feedback achieved high accuracies: 86.1% for size and 91.7% for compliance (chance level was 33.3%). Missing either feedback modality significantly degraded accuracy, proving their strong synergy.

For full trajectory collection in the tong task (T3), DITTO-X achieved a 70.0% success rate (versus 46.7% for Manus) while drastically cutting execution time from 85.5 seconds to 56.1 seconds. In the intervention task (T4), DITTO-X outperformed Manus by a wide margin, achieving 78.3% compared to Manus's 27.7%. With Manus, the mismatch between the operator's hand and the robot's hand at takeover frequently caused the robot to drop the tongs the moment control transferred.

### Policy Learning and DAgger Results
Even with initial pre-training demonstrations, policies trained on DITTO-X data outperformed those trained on Manus data. In the tong task, after grasping the tongs, the Manus policy succeeded in lifting the toy only 23.3% of the time, whereas the DITTO-X policy achieved 66.7%, reflecting more stable grip force control in the demonstrations.

In DAgger training, DITTO-X showed monotonic success rate improvements across rounds. In contrast, Manus policies actually degraded in performance because the jarring perturbations caused by takeover pose mismatches were learned directly by the policy. Furthermore, compared to a baseline that simply collected an equivalent number of demonstrations from the initial state, DAgger—which targeted failure states directly—achieved far higher final success rates.

Finally, successful policy learning was also demonstrated on the Wuji hand (drawer opening) and the lower-DoF Inspire hand, verifying the framework's versatility across diverse hardware.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: DITTO-X is a compelling teleoperation platform integrating multi-fingered force-haptic feedback with reverse teleoperation. Enabling high-quality demonstration collection and seamless policy intervention, it marks a major step forward for contact-rich robot learning.
sections.details:
DITTO-X provides multi-DoF force and haptic feedback while adapting flexibly to heterogeneous robot hands without custom redesigns. Crucially, its new "reverse teleoperation" mode—where the robot back-drives the human's hand—eliminates the physical discontinuities that occur when transferring control from autonomous execution to human intervention. This not only boosts the throughput of high-quality demonstration data collection, but also dramatically improves the effectiveness of DAgger cycles by enabling smooth human recoveries from policy failures.

With its hardware designs, control software, and over 1,800 demonstrations across three different hands released open-source, DITTO-X is expected to serve as a foundational platform for dexterous manipulation learning.

takeaways: In multi-finger teleoperation, relying solely on vision makes it impossible to sense contact forces or subtle slips; integrating dual-layer force and haptic feedback (sustained torque plus transient vibration) is indispensable.

During human interventions into autonomous policies, having the exoskeleton actively back-drive the human hand to match the robot's pose ("reverse teleoperation")—rather than asking the human to guess and match it—prevents dropping grasped objects.

When running DAgger on data that contains intervention-induced pose mismatches, policies can inadvertently learn the jarring takeover perturbations, causing performance to degrade across training rounds.
limitations: Because the ring and pinky fingers are coupled to the middle finger, the system cannot perform highly complex in-hand manipulation that requires independent 4th and 5th finger motion.

While safety mechanisms (torque and joint limits) exist for when a user resists motion during reverse teleoperation, exoskeleton motor tracking lag and glove fitting variations across hand sizes may affect the operational feel.
Although reverse teleoperation is implemented for the Wuji and Inspire hands, large-scale DAgger policy learning experiments were not evaluated on these two hands.
